**Day of the week:** February 29, 1960 was a Monday.

**The leap day itself is significant** — someone born on February 29 only has a "true" birthday every four years. In 2026, they would have had their leap day birthday on February 29... wait, 2026 is not a leap year. The most recent leap year was 2024. So their last "real" birthday was February 29, 2024, when they turned 64. Their next true leap day birthday will be February 29, 2028. 

As of September 5, 2026, they'd be 66, having only had around 16 actual February 29th birthdays despite that many calendar years passing, with the rest observed on Feb 28 or March 1.

Other February 29 dates come to mind too — I'm trying to recall if Hattie McDaniel's historic Oscar win for Gone with the Wind was actually on February 29, 1940, thinking through the 12th Academy Awards ceremony timing to confirm this.

1960 stands out as a pivotal year — Kennedy's election looming in November, seventeen African nations gaining independence, and just months later the FDA approving Enovid in May, launching the birth control pill era. I want the leap day theme woven throughout rather than mentioned just once, and I'm double-checking my memory that the 12th Academy Awards ceremony really was held on that date at the Ambassador Hotel.

I'm also considering the fragile U.S.-Soviet relationship in 1960, with the Powers U-2 incident derailing the planned Eisenhower-Khrushchev summit, and mapping out a life-arc lens for someone now 66 — tracing them from JFK's election through the Beatles, civil rights, Vietnam, the moon landing, Watergate, Reagan, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the internet age, and 9/11.

## February 29, 1960

You arrived on a Monday that the calendar conjures only once every four years.

---

**The day itself is the first fact.** February 29 exists because the Earth takes approximately 365.25 days to orbit the sun, and the calendar must periodically catch up with astronomy. The leap day is a correction — an acknowledgment that our neat human systems don't quite match the physical world. In 66 years of life, you have had exactly 16 true birthday celebrations on the actual date: 1964, 1968, 1972, and so on through 2024. Your next falls in 2028. There is something fitting about beginning on a day the calendar mostly pretends doesn't exist — it gives a particular relationship to time, to counting, to the strangeness of how we mark passage.

**On this exact date, twenty years earlier, history was made in a segregated hotel ballroom.** February 29, 1940: at the 12th Academy Awards, Hattie McDaniel became the first African American ever to win an Oscar — Best Supporting Actress for *Gone with the Wind* — and was seated at a segregated table at the side of the room. Twenty years to the day before your birth, that was where the country stood. By the time you arrived, the fight to change it was accelerating by the week.

**The sit-ins were 28 days old.** On February 1, 1960 — four weeks before your birth — four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina and refused to leave when denied service. By February 29, the movement had spread to more than thirty cities across the South. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee would form the following April. The Civil Rights Act was four years away. You were born into a country in open, active moral contest with itself, and that contest would define the decade of your childhood.

**The earth itself announced your birthday.** In the early hours of February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco — one of the deadliest natural disasters of the twentieth century. In under fifteen seconds, approximately 12,000 to 15,000 people were killed and the city was nearly erased. It made front pages worldwide. The day you arrived, the world was absorbing a catastrophe of almost incomprehensible speed. It is not a connection to celebrate, but it is the actual news of the day, and it gave your first hours a particular gravity.

**Three months after your birth, the world changed for women.** In May 1960, the FDA approved Enovid — the first oral contraceptive. The birth control pill. You were born just weeks before one of the most consequential medical and social decisions of the twentieth century, one that would reshape women's autonomy, family structure, career trajectories, and the entire landscape of modern life. By the time you were old enough to understand any of it, the world the pill made was already underway.

**You were born in an election year at a hinge.** Eisenhower's presidency was ending. In November 1960, a 43-year-old senator from Massachusetts named John Kennedy would narrowly defeat Richard Nixon in the first televised presidential election — the first in which what candidates *looked like* on a screen mattered as much as what they said. Kennedy's assassination would come when you were three years old. The images from that November weekend in Dallas are among the earliest collective memories of your generation.

**1960 was the Year of Africa.** Seventeen African nations gained independence that year — the largest single-year transfer of sovereignty on the continent in history. The map of the world was being redrawn as you arrived. Colonialism's formal structures were dismantling. The Non-Aligned Movement was asserting that the Cold War's binary wasn't the only frame available.

---

**The lifetime arc.** You grew up with the civil rights movement, Vietnam, the moon landing at nine years old, Watergate at fourteen. You came of age during the 1970s malaise and into Reagan's 1980s. The Berlin Wall fell when you were 29. The internet arrived in your thirties, the smartphone in your late forties. COVID at 60. Now at 66, in the middle of an AI transformation that began with theoretical work by a man — Alan Turing — who died six years before you were born.

---

You entered on a date that only fully arrives every 1,461 days — a small, precise reminder that the human calendar is an approximation, not a fact. The world you arrived into was also approximating: approximating equality, approximating peace, approximating its obligations to every person on its surface. Some of those approximations closed. Others remain open. The leap day keeps returning to check.
